title: China's long arm abroad
summary:
Right now, in courtrooms from Taipei to Los Angeles, people are being tried for doing the Chinese Communist Party's work inside other countries' governments. In May 2026 Eileen Wang, mayor of Arcadia, California, resigned and pleaded guilty to acting as an illegal agent of the People's Republic of China. In September 2026 Taiwan's High Court jailed Hu Peng-nien, a retired official of Taiwan's cabinet, for five years; prosecutors said he tried to recruit people for information on the military and on government work.

The United Front Work Department is a Communist Party body that builds influence over Chinese communities abroad and over foreign elites. On this map it mostly works through go-betweens: community associations, donors, 'friendship' groups and businesspeople. In Australia, developer Huang Xiangmo chaired a council for the 'peaceful reunification of China' and, with associates, gave about AU$2 million to Labor and over AU$1 million to the Liberal Party; the government cancelled his residency in 2019 on security-service advice. In Britain, MI5 warned MPs in 2022 that solicitor Christine Lee, a donor to Labour MP Barry Gardiner, had acted covertly with the department, and a tribunal later found the warning was issued for legitimate reasons.

A second route runs through police. In 2022 the rights group Safeguard Defenders listed 'overseas service stations' run by Chinese city police bureaus and used to pressure people wanted by China to go home. Ireland and the Netherlands ordered theirs shut, and a New York jury convicted a man over the Manhattan station in May 2026. In the Pacific, Chinese police now work openly inside local forces: Kiribati confirmed up to a dozen uniformed officers, and a 2022 pact lets the Solomon Islands ask for Chinese police and soldiers.

Not every case holds up. A judge acquitted former Canadian police officer William Majcher in May 2026, though prosecutors have appealed, and Britain dropped its case against parliamentary researcher Christopher Cash in October 2025.
implications: Influence here usually starts small: a donation, a campaign treasurer, a paid trip for village chiefs, an intern placed in a congressman's office. A voter sees a generous donor or a busy community leader, not the consulate or party office behind them. Much of the record comes from security-service warnings, expulsions and press reports rather than convictions, and several cases collapsed in court, so the line between lawful support for Beijing and covert work for it is often argued over. Things to watch now: the retrial of former New York governor's aide Linda Sun after her 2025 mistrial, the appeal of Majcher's acquittal, appeals in Taiwan's cases, and whether Solomon Islands prime minister Matthew Wale reviews the security pact with China as he promised.
uncertain: Many cases tie people to Chinese state proxies without showing that the United Front Work Department itself gave orders; New South Wales' corruption commission, for example, made no finding about the United Front. Several leading claims ended in acquittal, dismissal or dropped charges, and Safeguard Defenders revised its first police-station report after a legal scholar found factual errors.

title: Russia's networks in Europe and Africa
summary:
Right now Russia's defence ministry has about 2,000 troops in Mali, a base at Loumbila outside Burkina Faso's capital, a few hundred soldiers at an air base in Niger's capital, and up to 200 guarding Equatorial Guinea's president, Teodoro Obiang. In Italy, Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini's party, the Lega, still has a cooperation pact with United Russia, Vladimir Putin's ruling party. It was signed in 2017, and Il Foglio reported it renewed itself in 2022 to run until 2027.

The African side began with the Wagner Group, a private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin. From 2018 about 1,000 Wagner fighters guarded the Central African Republic's president, and a Russian, Valery Zakharov, became his security adviser. UN monitors counted up to 1,200 Wagner fighters with Khalifa Haftar's army in Libya in 2020. In 2023 the US sanctioned Mali's defence minister, saying he organised Wagner's arrival. After Prigozhin died that year, the ministry's Africa Corps took over most of these deployments. Prigozhin's strategists also worked on elections: in Madagascar in 2018 they dealt with up to eight candidates, one of whom said they handed him €5,000 in cash.

In Europe the tools are money, party pacts, energy company boards and the church. Austria's Freedom Party had its own United Russia pact from 2016 to 2021. Germany's former chancellor Gerhard Schröder chaired the board of Rosneft, Russia's state oil company, until 2022. Nathan Gill, a former British MEP, admitted taking bribes for pro-Russian speeches and was jailed for 10½ years in November 2025. In Moldova, the governor of Gagauzia got seven years in 2025 for financing a party with undeclared Russian money. Latvia, Estonia and Ukraine are cutting their Orthodox churches off from the Moscow Patriarchate, whose head backs the war in Ukraine. Not every case ends in a conviction: a Bulgarian court acquitted the pro-Russia leader Nikolay Malinov of spying in May 2026.
implications: Russia gains two kinds of reach. In parts of Africa its soldiers protect rulers and train armies, often for governments that took power in coups and sent French, US or UN forces away; reporting links some deployments to gold, diamond and timber deals. In Europe it works through people already inside politics, such as party leaders, MEPs and former ministers, whose payments or pacts voters usually learn about only after a raid, a leak or a trial. What people cannot easily see is who paid for a speech, an election observer or a social-media account. Worth watching: whether the Lega pact is ended before 2027, how the German case against the AfD's Petr Bystroň ends, and what Africa Corps receives from the governments it protects.
uncertain: The links between Wagner deployments and mining or timber concessions come from reporting, not court findings. In Madagascar the BBC found no evidence that the winner, Andry Rajoelina, took Russian money; Petr Bystroň denies receiving money and has not been charged; Nikolay Malinov was acquitted.

title: Governments buying officials in other countries

countries.note: The Chinese Communist Party's United Front Work Department directs 'united front' work among overseas Chinese and foreign elites.

In the 1970s the Korean Central Intelligence Agency and businessman Tongsun Park paid US congressmen ('Koreagate'); the House Fraser subcommittee (1978) also examined the KCIA's use of Sun Myung Moon's organisations.
The Russkiy Mir Foundation (2007) and the Voice of Europe network, sanctioned by the Czech government in March 2024 for paying European politicians.

summary:
Right now several governments are working to win over officials in other countries, and courts and inquiries keep catching pieces of it. In Canada, a public inquiry led by Justice Marie-Josée Hogue reported in January 2025 that proxies of India's government may have given, and may still give, illicit money to Canadian politicians to get pro-India candidates elected. A parliamentary committee had already said in 2024 that some unnamed MPs and senators were "semi-witting or witting" participants in foreign interference, naming China and Russia as the main states behind it. Canada expelled six Indian diplomats in October 2024 after the killing of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, and in 2025 listed the Lawrence Bishnoi gang, which officials said attacked targets Indian diplomats had pointed out, as a terrorist entity.

In the United States, Senator Bob Menendez, who chaired the committee that shapes US arms sales and aid, was convicted in 2024 of acting as an agent of Egypt and is in prison. Former congressman David Rivera was convicted in May 2026 of secretly lobbying for Venezuela's state oil company under a $50 million contract. Other cases ended without a verdict: Congressman Henry Cuellar was pardoned before trial over Azerbaijan money, New York mayor Eric Adams's case over Turkish favours was dismissed, and Tom Barrack, acquitted in 2022 of acting for the UAE, is now US ambassador to Turkey.

China's United Front Work Department, the Communist Party office that cultivates people abroad, appears in cases in Australia, Britain, Canada, the US and Taiwan. Russia appears through Hungarian MEP Béla Kovács, convicted of spying in 2022, and the Voice of Europe network the Czech government sanctioned in 2024.

This is not new. In the 1970s South Korea's intelligence agency, the KCIA, had businessman Tongsun Park hand cash to US congressmen; he admitted paying 30. Richard Hanna went to prison, three others were reprimanded, and Otto Passman was acquitted.
uncertain: Several cases ended without a conviction: Barrack and Passman were acquitted, the Adams case was dismissed, Cuellar was pardoned before trial, and the Canadian inquiries named no individual parliamentarian and found no "traitors". Saudi Arabia denies holding Lebanon's prime minister in 2017, the UAE denies arming Sudan's RSF, and India denies any role in the Nijjar killing; the 2026 US indictment of Bishnoi does not allege an Indian government role.

confirmed_by.title: Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference in Federal Electoral Processes and Democratic Institutions (Hogue), Canada, 2025
MI5 interference alert, January 2022; Investigatory Powers Tribunal, 2024
US House Subcommittee on International Organizations (Fraser), report, October 1978

implications: Influence bought from abroad travels through the same doors as ordinary lobbying: consulting contracts, donations, community associations, paid trips and help at election time. The official who takes the money may not know who is really behind it, and voters almost never can. What makes it visible is registration. Australia (2018), the UK (2023) and Canada (2024) passed laws requiring people acting for foreign states to register, and most of the US cases here turned on someone failing to register. Things to watch for: consulting contracts with foreign state companies, sudden clusters of donations, and officials pressing one country's interests on arms, sanctions or extraditions. Watch too how cases end, since several here closed through pardons or dropped charges rather than a verdict.

title: Foreign money inside Europe's parliaments
summary:
Several cases about foreign money inside Europe's parliaments are still open. The biggest is Qatargate in Brussels. Belgian prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid people in the European Parliament, the EU's elected assembly that votes on laws and budgets for 27 countries, to speak and vote in their favour. On 9 December 2022 police arrested Greek MEP Eva Kaili, then one of the Parliament's 14 vice-presidents, and found bags of cash at her home. Kaili is charged and denies it. Prosecutors say much of the money passed through Fight Impunity, a Brussels human-rights charity run by former Italian MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri, who took a plea deal in January 2023. In February 2026 the Brussels Court of Appeal ruled the case could go ahead. A second Belgian case concerns gifts allegedly given for positions favouring the Chinese telecoms company Huawei; eight people are charged.

The pattern was first exposed with Azerbaijan. The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) brings together MPs from 46 national parliaments and reports on elections and political prisoners. Leaked bank records published in 2017 showed about $2.9 billion moving through Danske Bank's Estonian branch in 2012–2014, some reaching people who defended Azerbaijan in PACE. A 2018 inquiry found members had broken its rules for Azerbaijan, and in 2021 a Milan court jailed former Italian MP Luca Volontè for four years for taking €2.39 million. That year the Bundestag lifted the immunity of two German MPs over Azerbaijani money.

Russia and China appear too. Former UK MEP Nathan Gill was sentenced in November 2025 to 10 years and 6 months for taking bribes to make pro-Russian statements. Hungarian MEP Béla Kovács was convicted in absentia of spying for Russia. German MEP Petr Bystroň is under investigation over a Russian-funded network and denies it, and an aide to MEP Maximilian Krah was jailed for spying for China.
implications: This route into government needs no election. A foreign state finds a few members who sit on the right committee or delegation and pays them through a charity, a company or cash handed over at a meeting. Voters see the speech or the vote; they do not see who paid for it. The cases show small assemblies such as PACE are a favoured target, because their reports on elections and political prisoners count abroad but get little attention at home. The members caught come from centre-right, socialist and nationalist parties alike, and the paying states include Qatar, Morocco, Azerbaijan, Russia and China. Watch the Qatargate and Huawei trials in Belgium, the Bystroň inquiry in Germany, and whether parliaments tighten their rules on charities, gifts and side income.
uncertain: Most people named in the Qatargate, Huawei and Voice of Europe cases are charged or investigated, not convicted, and they deny wrongdoing; one MEP named in the Huawei case turned out to share a name with the man who received gifts, and Parliament kept his immunity. The 2018 PACE inquiry found 'strong suspicions' and breaches of its code of conduct, which is not a court verdict.

title: Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement
roles: Country that handed people over or closed schools
summary:
Turkey's government is still reaching across borders for people it links to the Gülen movement. In October 2024 Kenya sent four Turkish refugees back to Turkey 'at the request of the government of Türkiye', in the words of a Kenyan official; the UN said it was 'deeply concerned'. The Gülen movement, also called Hizmet, is a religious movement led by the preacher Fethullah Gülen that built schools and charities in many countries. Turkey calls it a terrorist group, 'FETÖ', and blames it for the failed coup of 15 July 2016.

The quarrel began in December 2013, when Istanbul prosecutors opened a corruption case reaching Prime Minister Erdoğan's inner circle. The government called it a plot by Gülen followers inside the police and courts, sacked the prosecutors. After the 2016 coup attempt it went much further: 2,745 judges were removed in one day, about 23,000 police were dismissed by the end of 2017, about 15,000 military personnel by 2019, and about 150,000 public employees in all.

Abroad, Turkey asked governments to close Gülen-linked schools. Senegal, Chad, Niger, Guinea, Somalia, Sudan and Pakistan handed theirs to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation; Azerbaijan's state oil company took over its schools; Kazakhstan declined. People were also taken: Malaysia deported three men, Kosovo flew six to Turkey, Moldova sent seven, and a schools head vanished from Kyrgyzstan. Kosovo later jailed its intelligence chief for the deportations, and the European Court of Human Rights ruled Moldova's transfers illegal. Interpol refused 773 Turkish requests for wanted notices as political. Turkey's state religious office, the Diyanet, which runs over 2,000 mosques abroad, gave parliament reports on Gülen followers in 38 countries.

An older thread runs through the Grey Wolves, youth wing of the nationalist MHP. The 1996 Susurluk car crash put an MP, a police chief and a wanted Grey Wolves gunman in one car. France dissolved the Grey Wolves in 2020, and that ban stays in force.
implications: A state can use its own police, intelligence service, religious office and diplomatic weight to pursue people living legally in other countries. Ordinary residents abroad, such as teachers, refugees and families of the accused, can be detained with little warning when their host government agrees to a request it never explains in public. Many governments complied quietly; a few, like Kazakhstan, Mongolia and Kosovo's courts, pushed back. The movement itself also worked on foreign governments: groups tied to it paid for about 200 trips to Turkey for US members of Congress and staff. Watch for further handovers from countries that host refugees, court rulings against them, and how host states treat Diyanet-employed imams.
uncertain: Whether the Gülen movement planned the 2016 coup attempt is decided by Turkish courts, and the movement denies it; most of those dismissed in the purges were never tried. German prosecutors could not prove that DITIB imams spied for Turkey, and Turkey's role in the Mongolia abduction attempt rests on press reports.

title: Churches and movements placing members in the state
summary:
Today members of religious movements hold some of the highest offices in several countries, while in others the state is breaking such movements up. In Japan the courts have ordered the Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, dissolved; the Tokyo High Court upheld the order on 4 March 2026 after a lower court found 1,559 victims of unlawful donation drives. The church's ties to the ruling Liberal Democratic Party go back to 1968, when former prime minister Nobusuke Kishi co-founded its political arm, and the party's own 2022 survey found 179 of its 379 lawmakers had dealings with it. In South Korea a court jailed church leader Han Hak-ja in August 2026 for gifts to the then first lady and money to a ruling-party lawmaker; the church said it would appeal. The founder of another church, Shincheonji, was indicted in July 2026 after at least 56,472 followers were signed up to the People Power Party.

Elsewhere the placement is open and lawful. Chile's president, José Antonio Kast, was raised in the Catholic Schoenstatt movement, and his under-secretary of justice is a numerary, a celibate member, of Opus Dei. In 2020, 38 of 53 BJP ministers in India had roots in the RSS, the Hindu nationalist volunteer body. In Brazil the evangelical caucus lists 213 of 513 deputies, and bishops of the Universal Church lead the Republicanos party.

The pattern has older roots. Opus Dei members ran Franco's finance and trade ministries in Spain from 1957, and eleven members of his 1969 cabinet had ties to it. In the 1970s Scientology planted members inside the US tax service; eleven were convicted. Turkey shows the reverse: after the 2016 coup attempt the state blamed the Gülen movement, an Islamic network that had placed school graduates in the police and courts, dismissed about 150,000 public employees, and pressed governments from Pakistan to Kenya to hand over its schools and people.
uncertain: Many cases here rest on membership or reported ties alone; membership of Opus Dei, the RSS or Nippon Kaigi is not secret and is not misconduct, and some people named, such as those linked to El Yunque in Mexico, deny belonging. The scale of Gülen placement inside the Turkish state is documented mainly by Turkish government proceedings that critics say also swept up non-members.

Tokyo District Court dissolution order, 25 March 2025
US v. Mary Sue Hubbard et al., D.D.C., 1979
Turkish government decrees under the 2016 state of emergency

implications: Belonging to a church or movement while holding office is lawful, and many democracies welcome religious citizens in government. The concern begins when a movement's own leaders, not voters or the civil service, decide who rises and what they do once there: when a church signs tens of thousands of followers up to a party, supplies campaign volunteers, or tells members how to vote as a bloc, as the Iglesia ni Cristo does in the Philippines. Voters usually cannot see these arrangements. Turkey shows the danger running the other way: once a government decides a movement has infiltrated it, it can remove tens of thousands at once. Things to watch for: mass party sign-ups, bloc endorsements, church volunteers in campaigns, and dismissals justified by membership alone.

title: Religious nationalism in power
summary:
In two of Asia's largest democracies, members of religious-nationalist movements hold the top offices today. India's prime minister, Narendra Modi, spent years as a full-time organiser for the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer group founded in 1925 whose political wing grew into the ruling BJP. India's vice president since September 2025, C. P. Radhakrishnan, has been with the RSS since he was 16. In 2020 the news site ThePrint counted 38 of the 53 BJP ministers in Modi's government with RSS roots.

In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has served in the parliamentary league of Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby that campaigns to revise the constitution. When her cabinet took office in October 2025, the Communist Party's paper listed 10 of 19 ministers in that league and 12 in the league of the Shinto Political League, the political arm of the shrine association. Under Shinzo Abe in 2014 the reported counts were 15 and 16 of 19.

Further south, Buddhist nationalist monks got close to power. Sri Lanka's Bodu Bala Sena ('Buddhist Power Force') is a monks' group accused of stirring anti-Muslim violence. In 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who as defence secretary had opened its training centre in 2013, put its leader Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara in charge of a task force on legal reform. Gnanasara is back in prison: on 10 September 2026 the Supreme Court voided the 2019 presidential pardon of his contempt sentence. In Myanmar, four laws on conversion, marriage and birth spacing passed in 2015 were drafted from texts proposed by the monks' group Ma Ba Tha, and the military government gave the monk Wirathu one of the country's highest honours in 2022.

Hizb ut-Tahrir, which calls for a single worldwide caliphate, works from outside instead, recruiting officers. Pakistan's army convicted a brigadier over it in 2012, Bangladesh's army said it stopped a coup plot that year, and Britain banned the group in 2024.
implications: These movements are mostly lawful and open, and their members win elections. The point to understand is that a cabinet and a movement can be largely the same people, so a movement's aims, such as constitutional revision in Japan, a single legal code in Sri Lanka or rules on conversion and marriage in Myanmar, can arrive as government policy without a public debate about the movement itself. Membership lists are often unpublished; the RSS keeps none, so counts come from journalists. Religious minorities tend to feel the effects first. Watch who sits on cabinet committees, who drafts laws on religion and family, and whether courts can still undo political favours, as Sri Lanka's did in 2026.
uncertain: The cabinet counts in Japan and India come from press reporting and membership lists, not official findings, and the count for Takaichi's reshuffled September 2026 cabinet has not been checked. Belonging to the RSS, Nippon Kaigi or the Shinto league is lawful and does not show that the group directed any government decision.

title: Governments that export religion
roles: Where the mosques or churches are
summary:
Several governments run or pay for places of worship in other countries, and the countries hosting them are now pushing back. Turkey's Diyanet is the state religious directorate: it employs imams as civil servants and runs over 2,000 mosques abroad, through branches such as DITIB in Germany and ATIB in Austria. Saudi Arabia worked through the Muslim World League, and Russia through the Russian Orthodox Church (Moscow Patriarchate), whose head, Patriarch Kirill, backs the war in Ukraine.

The break with the Russian church is the sharpest today. Latvia's parliament made its Orthodox Church independent of any outside church authority in 2022. Estonia refused to renew the residence permit of the Moscow Patriarchate's metropolitan, who left in February 2024, and tightened its churches law in 2025. Ukraine passed a law in August 2024 banning the Russian church and giving affiliated bodies nine months to cut ties. Britain, Canada and Ukraine have sanctioned Kirill since 2022; an EU listing was dropped when Hungary objected.

The mosque cases show how these ties came to light. After the failed coup in Turkey in July 2016, the Diyanet told its imams abroad to gather information on followers of the Gülen movement and gave parliament 50 reports from 38 countries. German prosecutors opened a case against DITIB imams in 2017; a court later said spying could not be proved, and the interior ministry cut DITIB's federal funding in 2018. Austria, which bans foreign funding of religious bodies, put about 40 ATIB imams' residence permits under review that year. Belgium had lent the Great Mosque of Brussels to Saudi Arabia in 1967 on a 99-year rent-free lease; it ended the arrangement in 2018, then in 2020 blocked a new management body after its security service found members tied to Moroccan intelligence and to the Diyanet. A Dutch parliamentary inquiry in 2020 found donors from four Gulf states funding hardline Salafi teaching in mosques.
implications: For a sponsoring state, a network of mosques or churches abroad is a way to reach people from home living overseas: to pick the preachers, shape the teaching and, in the Turkish case, to gather names of its opponents. For a congregation, it is often hard to tell where the money and the instructions come from. Host governments answer with funding bans, residence permits and church laws, and the sponsoring state may call that an attack on religion, as Turkey did in Austria. Worth watching: how Ukraine's ban is applied to individual parishes, whether any Orthodox church recognises Latvia's independent church, and how host states pay imams once foreign money is cut off.
uncertain: Germany's spying case against DITIB imams could not be proved in court. Funding and appointing clergy is not the same as directing the host country's government, and the record shows influence over congregations rather than over host-state officials.
case_role: Where the mosques or churches are

title: Consultants and lobbyists inside the ministries
summary:
Private advisers now work inside governments on a large scale. The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, a London non-profit, reports placing advisers in more than 45 governments and had about 1,000 staff in 2026; in Rwanda it has helped run strategy and delivery units in the president's and prime minister's offices. Its largest donor is Larry Ellison's foundation, which gave over £52 million in 2023. In France, prosecutors announced a €65 million seizure in September 2026 in a tax-fraud money-laundering inquiry into McKinsey, a US management-consulting firm.

The clearest record comes from South Africa. The Zondo Commission into state capture found that President Jacob Zuma, tax chief Tom Moyane and the consultancy Bain & Company worked together to take over the revenue service, SARS, whose investigators were seen as a threat. Bain denies 'wilfully' helping; the Treasury barred it from state contracts for 10 years in 2022. McKinsey admitted in a 2024 agreement with the US Justice Department that it conspired to bribe officials at the state power and rail companies, and agreed to pay $122.85 million. KPMG withdrew a report that had fed charges against a former finance minister, and nine executives resigned.

The same door swings in rich countries. In 2013 a UK parliamentary committee found Big Four accounting firms lent staff to the Treasury to help write tax law, then advised clients on it. In Australia a PwC partner shared confidential Treasury tax plans with at least 53 partners. Leaked Uber files show economy minister Emmanuel Macron helped the company in France, which he says he is proud of. Former UK prime minister David Cameron texted the Chancellor for Greensill Capital; inquiries found he broke no rules. In 2025 an EU court annulled the Commission's refusal to release Ursula von der Leyen's texts with Pfizer's chief, and in Canada an ethics commissioner found Justin Trudeau broke conflict law over SNC-Lavalin.
implications: Consultants, accountants and lobbyists are hired openly, but the work they do inside a ministry is rarely published. The same firm can help write a tax law and then sell advice on getting round it, or help reorganise a tax office whose investigators were looking at the firm's clients' friends. Citizens cannot see the contracts, the texts or the seminars, so the record usually comes from leaks, parliamentary inquiries and court cases years later. The firms that pay penalties tend to keep working elsewhere: the UK lifted its ban on Bain two years early. Watch which outside advisers sit in your government's central offices, who pays for them, and whether ministers' messages with companies are kept.
uncertain: Most cases end in findings by inquiries, ombudsmen or ethics officers, not criminal convictions; McKinsey's admissions came through a deferred prosecution agreement. Bain says the allegations are unproven, and neither the Uber Files nor the Pfizer texts show a payment to an official. Nothing in the dossier says the Tony Blair Institute's work is improper; it shows only its scale and funding.

title: Global firms buying governments
summary:
Some of the biggest cases on this map have nothing to do with secret societies. They are companies paying the people who run governments, and several are still working through the courts. Michael Madigan, for decades Speaker of the Illinois House, began a 7½-year sentence in October 2025 after Chicago's electricity company, Commonwealth Edison, gave jobs and contracts to his associates to win support for its bills; an appeals court upheld the conviction in April 2026. Malaysia's former prime minister Najib Razak was sentenced to 15 years in December 2025 over more than $1 billion in his personal accounts tied to 1MDB, a state investment fund whose bond deals Goldman Sachs bankers arranged; he is appealing. In New York, Indian tycoon Gautam Adani faces charges of paying more than $250 million to Indian officials for solar power contracts, which he denies.

The longest story is Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group that admitted in 2016 to paying $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries through a department set up for that purpose. Ecuador's vice-president Jorge Glas got six years in 2017; Peru's former president Alejandro Toledo got 20 years in 2024 for about $35 million tied to a highway contract. Not every verdict stood: Brazil's Supreme Court annulled Lula da Silva's convictions in 2021 because the court that tried him lacked jurisdiction.

Swiss commodity traders, which buy and sell oil and metals worldwide, appear too. Glencore admitted bribery in Nigeria and four other African states and agreed to pay over $1 billion; Gunvor was convicted in Switzerland over Ecuador, and Trafigura over Brazil and Angola, with the Angola ruling under appeal.

Sometimes a company reaches for the cabinet itself. South Africa's deputy finance minister Mcebisi Jonas said the Gupta brothers, businessmen close to President Jacob Zuma, offered him the finance ministry in 2015; the Zondo inquiry found ministers and state-company heads acted corruptly for the family, who deny it.
implications: Here access is bought with cash, jobs or contracts. The cost lands on the public: the bribe is built into the price of the highway, oil deal or power contract, and the law that follows can favour the payer, as with Ohio's $1 billion-plus rescue of FirstEnergy's nuclear plants, which brought its House Speaker 20 years in prison. Most of these cases came to light in foreign courts, especially in the United States and Switzerland, rather than in the country where officials took the money. Things to watch: Najib's and Trafigura's appeals, the Adani case, the long-running charges against former Mexican state oil chief Emilio Lozoya, and former leaders taking board seats at other countries' state companies.
uncertain: Company settlements and guilty pleas often name countries and amounts without naming the officials paid, as in Glencore's Congo settlement. Several individual cases are unresolved or contested: Lula's convictions were annulled, Adani and Lozoya deny the charges and have not been tried, and the Guptas deny offering ministries.

title: Spyware and elections for hire
summary:
Elections in several African countries have become work for hire, with foreign firms selling campaign data, fake online accounts and hacking. Most of the firms named here have closed or been blacklisted, but the methods are still on offer. The best-known is Cambridge Analytica, a British data firm that was part of SCL Group. In an undercover Channel 4 recording broadcast in March 2018, its managing director said it ran Uhuru Kenyatta's winning campaigns in Kenya in 2013 and 2017, 'rebranded the party twice' and wrote its manifesto. Leaked emails published in 2023 showed it worked with an Israeli outfit, Team Jorge, in Nigeria's 2015 election on a campaign to discredit Muhammadu Buhari, who won anyway. Cambridge Analytica closed in 2018.

Team Jorge was led by Tal Hanan, a former special-forces operative filmed by undercover reporters in 2023. He claimed work on 33 presidential elections and showed access to the Telegram account of Dennis Itumbi, digital strategist for William Ruto in Kenya's 2022 election; Itumbi confirmed it had been compromised. Another Israeli firm, Archimedes Group, was removed by Facebook in 2019 for fake networks aimed at African elections including Nigeria's, after spending about $1.1 million on ads.

Russia's version came from Yevgeny Prigozhin's political strategists. In October 2019 Facebook took down almost 200 fake accounts tied to him that targeted eight African countries and meddled in Mozambique's and Madagascar's elections. A Prigozhin-linked group called AFRIC sent about 40 'election observers' to Zimbabwe's 2018 vote.

Spyware sits beside this trade. NSO Group, an Israeli company, sells its Pegasus phone-hacking tool only to governments. In 2021 a consortium of journalists reported that Morocco had selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones, including politicians and senior officers, as targets. Morocco denied it. The US put NSO on a trade blacklist that November.
implications: A voter usually never sees these firms. The posts look local, the observers look independent, and the data work is hidden behind a branding contract. The people who gain are the candidates and governments who can pay, and the foreign firms or states that then hold their secrets. Spyware bought by one government can be turned on another country's leaders, as Algeria said of Morocco when it cut diplomatic ties in 2021. Watch for unexplained consulting contracts in campaign spending, sudden networks of new accounts before a vote, and observer missions nobody has heard of.
uncertain: Most of these cases rest on undercover recordings, leaked emails and platform takedown reports rather than court findings. Morocco denies using Pegasus, and no court here has ruled that hired help changed an election's result.

title: Scam compounds and casino money inside Asian states
summary:
In Cambodia and the Philippines, scam compounds and online gambling businesses reached into government offices, and both countries are now prosecuting or shutting them down. The Philippine cases involve POGOs, Chinese-run online gambling firms licensed from 2016 to serve players in China. Senate hearings in 2024 tied many of them to fraud, human trafficking and torture. Alice Guo, elected mayor of the town of Bamban in 2022, was linked to a POGO hub raided there. A court later ruled she is a Chinese citizen, Guo Hua Ping, and voided her election; on 20 November 2025 she was convicted of qualified human trafficking and sentenced to life. Harry Roque, once President Rodrigo Duterte's spokesman, faces arrest warrants over a hub in Pampanga; he denies being its lawyer and has sought asylum in the Netherlands. President Marcos ordered every POGO closed by the end of 2024, and Congress made the ban law in October 2025.

In Cambodia the money reached closer to the top. Chen Zhi, born in China's Fujian province, became a Cambodian citizen in 2014, built the Prince Group into one of the country's largest conglomerates, and served as an adviser to Hun Sen and other leaders. In October 2025 the US Justice Department indicted him for fraud and money laundering, calling him head of a cyber-fraud empire run from scam compounds, and seized about 127,271 bitcoin, worth about US$14 billion. In January 2026 Cambodia said it had arrested him, revoked his citizenship and sent him to China. Huione Group, a Phnom Penh firm whose payment arm has Prime Minister Hun Manet's cousin Hun To as a director, lost its banking licence in March 2025. The US Treasury found it had laundered over US$4 billion, including money from North Korean hackers and scam operations.
implications: Scam compounds need protection: licences, local officials who look away, and banks that move the money. When their owners advise national leaders, or a leader's relative sits on their board, the state's own power can shield them. The people who pay are the workers trafficked into compounds and the victims defrauded abroad, while nearby residents may see only a new compound or a generous local donor. What to watch: whether the Philippine ban holds, how Chen Zhi's case proceeds in China, and whether any Cambodian official tied to him or to Huione is investigated at home.
uncertain: Harry Roque has only been charged and Chen Zhi only indicted; neither has been tried. The record shows business and advisory ties to Cambodia's leaders, not that those leaders knew of or directed the fraud.

title: Iran's armed allies inside governments
roles: Where they sit in the state
summary:
In Lebanon and Iraq, armed groups backed by Iran sit inside the state they share power with. In Lebanon, Hezbollah, a Shia party with its own armed wing, holds about 14 of 128 seats in parliament, and its picks run the health and labour ministries in the government Prime Minister Nawaf Salam formed in February 2025; with its ally Amal it controls six of 24 portfolios. At least 28 countries, including the US and UK, list it as a terrorist group. On 7 August 2025 the cabinet approved the aim that only the state should hold weapons, and Hezbollah- and Amal-aligned ministers walked out. In September the army presented a plan to disarm all militias, chiefly Hezbollah, with no timeline. Hezbollah's leader Naim Qassem rejects disarmament.

In Iraq the route was a law. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) formed in June 2014 to fight Islamic State from about 67 mostly Shia factions, almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards. A 2016 law made them part of Iraq's armed forces, under the prime minister and paid from the state budget. Kata'ib Hezbollah, which the US listed as a terrorist group in 2009, staffs three PMF brigades. In 2024 the PMF chief of staff said it took orders from Iran's supreme leader. Falih al-Fayyadh, sanctioned by the US in 2021 over the killing of protesters, remains PMF chairman. A 2025 bill to tighten state control was tabled under US pressure.

The network reaches further. In 2013 a Kenyan court jailed two Iranians alleged to be members of the Quds Force, the Revolutionary Guards' foreign branch, over explosives. In 2023 the US sanctioned Paraguay's former president Horacio Cartes and sitting vice-president Hugo Velázquez for corruption, saying both had ties to members of Hezbollah; the US lifted the sanctions on Cartes in 2025.
implications: Here an outside power does not need secret members; its allies hold ministries, seats and state-paid brigades in the open. People in Lebanon and Iraq pay taxes that fund forces which answer, by their own commanders' statements, partly to Tehran, and decisions on war can be taken outside cabinet. The US sanctions officials it accuses, but that is itself a foreign government's judgement, and sanctions can be lifted. Watch whether Lebanon's disarmament plan gets a timeline, whether Iraq passes the PMF reform bill, and who controls the ministries that hand out jobs and services.
uncertain: The US sanctions are administrative findings, not court verdicts, and the Paraguay sanctions say only that the two men had ties to Hezbollah members. The Kenyan men were alleged, not proven, to be Quds Force members. The dossier does not show how much day-to-day control Iran exercises over each group.

title: Private forums where officials meet money
summary:
Many of the people running Western governments today also sit in a handful of private forums. In June 2025 the Bilderberg Meeting, a yearly conference of about 130 politicians, executives and academics whose discussions are kept off the record, met in Stockholm. Its list named Greece's prime minister, Finland's president, NATO's secretary general, five European Commissioners, Britain's health secretary and two US regional military commanders; Sweden's prime minister attended without being listed. The World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, which picks about 100 people under 40 a year, took sitting ministers from Angola, India, the Netherlands and South Africa into recent classes.

In the United States some forums write policy as well as host it. The American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) has state legislators and corporate members draft 'model bills' together; about 850 of them were published in 2011, and Arizona's 2010 immigration law was drafted at an ALEC meeting. The Federalist Society, a network of conservative lawyers, helped choose judges: 43 of Trump's first 51 appeals-court nominees were members, and in May 2025 Trump called it his 'recommending source' before turning on its former leader. Authors of the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 plan hold senior posts in his second administration. Under Biden, nearly 70 staff from the Democratic-leaning Center for American Progress had moved into the administration by mid-2021.

The roots go back a century. During the Second World War the Council on Foreign Relations wrote 682 confidential memos for the State Department, and a 1977 study found its members held over half of the senior US foreign-policy posts it surveyed between 1945 and 1972. When Trilateral Commission member Jimmy Carter took office in 1977, fellow members became his secretaries of state and defence. The Atlas Network of free-market think tanks has seen its people become ministers in Chile and Australia.
uncertain: No forum here has been shown to have decided a government policy itself; the cases are memberships, placements, model bills and recommendations. Figures such as the IEA's claim about Boris Johnson's cabinet and Atlas's credit for Javier Milei's reforms are the organisations' own claims.

confirmed_by.title: Christian Science Monitor, 1980, on Trilateral Commission members in the Carter administration
ALEC Exposed (Center for Media and Democracy), 2011

implications: Membership of these forums is usually public and lawful; the names are printed. What stays private is the conversation. Officials who regulate banks, sign defence deals or pick judges spend days with executives and with each other, off the record, and the same circle meets again under the next government. Ordinary voters, small businesses and most opposition parties have no seat. In the United States the effect is more direct: a model bill or a list of judges can arrive already written. Watch which ministers attend each year's Bilderberg, whether a bill in your state matches an ALEC model, and who drafted the plan a new administration follows.

summary:
International bodies are meant to stand above any one government, but governments and industries work inside them. Interpol, the agency police forces use to send each other wanted-person alerts, shows it most clearly. In 2021 it elected Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, inspector general of the UAE Interior Ministry, as president. The UAE had given donations reported at about $54 million, roughly what the other 194 members pay in fees combined. Britons Matthew Hedges and Ali Issa Ahmad accuse Al-Raisi of responsibility for their torture in UAE custody, and in 2022 French anti-terrorism prosecutors opened a preliminary inquiry; he denies it and served until November 2025. His predecessor, Meng Hongwei, was also China's vice-minister of public security; he vanished on a trip home in 2018 and was jailed for 13½ years for bribery. Interpol refused 773 Turkish requests aimed at Gülen suspects, withdrew a Bahraini notice that got a refugee footballer arrested in Bangkok, and in 2022 stopped Russia sending alerts directly.

Health is the second arena. A WHO-commissioned expert committee found in 2000 that tobacco companies had worked for years, often invisibly, to undermine WHO tobacco policy, including through consultants. In 2010 a Council of Europe resolution criticised the secrecy of WHO's H1N1 vaccine advice. The Gates Foundation was WHO's second-largest funder in 2020, mostly for programmes it chooses.

Other cases run the opposite way, from the body into a government. A World Bank managing director became Nigeria's finance minister; an IMF official became Pakistan's central bank governor while Pakistan negotiated an IMF loan. In 2021 an inquiry found Kristalina Georgieva, as World Bank chief executive, pressed staff to raise China's business ranking; she denied it and leads the IMF. In sport, officeholders were convicted in bribery cases: Honduras's former president Rafael Callejas, Brazil's former São Paulo governor José Maria Marin, and Carlos Nuzman, head of Rio's 2016 bid.
uncertain: Interpol's rules forbid political notices and it refused many of the requests described, so much of the record is attempted misuse. The torture complaints against Al-Raisi are under preliminary inquiry, and the IMF board said the evidence against Georgieva was not conclusive. Neither the Council of Europe nor the dossier found proven pharmaceutical control of WHO, and Gates funding is shown, not wrongdoing.

implications: These bodies exist so countries can trust shared rules: a wanted notice, a health warning, a country ranking. When a member government leads or funds the body, it can try to turn those tools on its critics, and the person affected may be a dissident stopped at a foreign airport who never learns why. When an industry or a private donor shapes priorities, the advice reaches health ministries that copy it. The checks that worked here came from inside rules and outside pressure: Interpol's refugee and political-notice rules, French prosecutors, US courts. Watch who funds, staffs and leads these bodies, and whether they publish their decisions.

title: Movements that sought the state itself

countries.note: A military court convicted Brigadier Ali Khan and four majors in 2012 of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir.
The army said in January 2012 it had stopped a coup by serving and retired officers linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir.

summary:
Today the Muslim Brotherhood is being pushed out of governments it once helped run. In January 2026 the United States listed branches of the Brotherhood as terrorists for the first time: the Egyptian, Jordanian and Lebanese branches. Jordan had already banned the group in April 2025, even though its political party, the Islamic Action Front, had won 31 of 138 seats the year before and was the largest party in parliament. In Tunisia, Rached Ghannouchi, former speaker of parliament and leader of the Ennahda party, is in prison, with a further 22-year sentence handed down in February 2025 and another 14 years in July 2025; his party calls the cases political.

The Muslim Brotherhood is a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928, with branches across the region. Unlike most groups on this map, it often stood for election openly, and won. Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, became Egypt's president in 2012; the army removed him in July 2013, and that December the government declared the Brotherhood a terrorist organisation. Ennahda, which grew out of the Brotherhood tradition but says it has no organisational link to it, led Tunisia's government from 2011 to 2014. Morocco's Brotherhood-inspired PJD led the government for ten years until it lost 113 seats in 2021. In Sudan, the Brotherhood-derived National Islamic Front helped Omar al-Bashir seize power in 1989, and in 2025 the US sanctioned Sudan's finance minister and an Islamist militia fighting beside the army, using the word 'Islamist' rather than 'Brotherhood'.

The second movement, Hizb ut-Tahrir, founded in 1953, calls openly for a single caliphate. In two countries it reached into the army. Pakistan's military court convicted a brigadier and four majors of links to it in 2012, and Bangladesh's army named it among those behind a coup plot it stopped that year. Indonesia banned it in 2017, and Britain made membership a crime in January 2024.
uncertain: Whether a given officeholder acted on the movement's instructions is rarely established in court, and parties named here, including Ennahda, Morocco's PJD and the UAE's Islah, deny organisational ties to the Brotherhood. Some designations came after elections the movements had won, and some actions taken against them, such as Austria's raids, were later overturned.

confirmed_by.title: Egyptian cabinet designation, 25 December 2013
Pakistan Army field general court martial, August 2012

implications: In this pattern the question is less who is hidden inside a government than who is allowed into it. When the Brotherhood won elections, its people took office in the open; its opponents later described them as infiltrators and removed them, in Egypt by a coup. In Jordan the largest party in parliament now sits beside a banned parent movement. The label is also used broadly: Austria's 2020 raids on suspected Brotherhood networks were later ruled unlawful, and a 2025 French state report warned of Brotherhood 'entryism' in local politics while finding no recent document showing a wish to set up an Islamic state in France. Watch what happens to the Islamic Action Front's seats, and whether other governments follow the US designations.

title: Lodges inside police forces and courts
summary:
Since December 2025, officers and staff of London's Metropolitan Police have had to declare if they are Freemasons. By February 2026, 397 had done so, most of them Freemasons. The United Grand Lodge of England, the governing body of English Freemasonry, went to court to stop the rule; in February 2026 a High Court judge refused, calling it a proportionate way to keep public trust in policing.

Freemasonry is a private fraternity organised in lodges, and police officers and judges are supposed to owe loyalty only to the law. A person who is arrested or tried cannot tell whether the officer or judge shares a private oath with the other side. Journalist Stephen Knight's book The Brotherhood (1983–84) described lodges inside the police. In 1988 a Leicester shop owner and his son were assaulted at a ladies' night of a Blackburn lodge whose members were mostly serving officers; the father and son, not their attackers, were charged, then acquitted, and the Chief Constable paid most of a £170,000 settlement. A Commons committee urged a register in 1997, and from 1998 new judges and police had to declare membership. The rule for judges was dropped in 2009, when a review found 5.4% of judges were masons and no evidence of impropriety.

Italy shows the stakes more sharply. In 1981 police seized the list of Propaganda Due (P2), a secret lodge run by Licio Gelli: it included the heads of all three intelligence services, the commander of the financial police and 195 military officers. A 1982 law banned secret societies that interfere with public bodies, and in 2018 it was used to convict members of the 'P3' network, a case in which a former head of Italy's top court got a suspended sentence for abuse of office. In the United States, the 1920s Ku Klux Klan enrolled Denver's police chief, and in 2014 a Florida deputy chief resigned over past Klan ties.
uncertain: How far lodge ties changed particular promotions, arrests or verdicts is rarely proven case by case. UK inquiries found the belief damaging but no systematic conspiracy, and the 2021 Daniel Morgan panel found no evidence Masonic channels were used corruptly in that case.

confirmed_by.title: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, Freemasonry in the Police and the Judiciary, 1997; Freemasonry in Public Life, 1999
Italian Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission, report on Freemasonry, December 2017

implications: Belonging to a lawful lodge is not wrongdoing. The problem the record shows is visibility. Britain's parliament said it got cooperation from the Grand Lodge only 'through compulsion', and it took five attempts to produce a list of masons in one disbanded police squad. Italy learned who sat in P2 only because a search for something else found the list. Where membership is not declared, people facing police or courts cannot judge whether a hidden loyalty is in play, even when none is. The current direction in Britain is toward disclosure for police and away from it for judges. Watch whether other forces follow the Met, and how undeclared memberships are handled, such as the Romanian ministers named in 2019.

title: French lodges and African presidencies
roles: Head of state or minister in a lodge
case_role: Head of state or minister in a lodge

countries.note: The Grande Loge Nationale Française and the Grand Orient de France sponsored or chartered lodges in former colonies; the GLNF's grand master installed Ali Bongo as grand master of Gabon's lodge in 2009. Jacques Foccart's Service d'Action Civique ran France's African networks from the Élysée.

summary:
In several former French colonies, Masonic lodges linked to Paris still sit close to the presidency. In Gabon, the grand mastership of the national lodge traditionally went to the head of state. After the August 2023 coup that removed Ali Bongo, the lodge passed it to a provincial governor; coup leader Brice Oligui Nguema reportedly declined it. Gabonreview, citing Africa Intelligence, reported that in November 2023 the head of the Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body, met Oligui in secret and offered support; Oligui was elected president in April 2025. In the Republic of Congo, President Denis Sassou-Nguesso is reported to be grand master of a lodge linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Française (GLNF).

The roots are French. Between 1901 and 1904 the War Ministry used reports collected through Grand Orient lodges to sort 18,818 army officers for promotion, favouring republicans and blocking Catholics; when it came out, the minister resigned and the government fell. Later, Jacques Foccart, de Gaulle's adviser on Africa, co-founded the Service d'Action Civique, a Gaullist militia dissolved in 1982 after its members murdered a police inspector and his family.

In Africa, Omar Bongo, president of Gabon from 1967 to 2009, founded two lodges, one tied to each French body, and led them until he died. In 2009 the GLNF's grand master installed his son Ali in the post, the year Ali became president. A 2012 Jeune Afrique survey named Blaise Compaoré of Burkina Faso as a former grand master succeeded by his foreign minister, and said the presidents of Mali and Guinea oversaw national lodges and Senegal's Abdoulaye Wade had been initiated. Chad's Idriss Déby, Niger's Mamadou Tandja and the Central African Republic's François Bozizé were reported as members. Le Monde reported in 1999 that Cameroon's Paul Biya gave tens of millions of francs to a French Templar order, OSTI.
uncertain: Most memberships here come from journalists, mainly Jeune Afrique, not from the lodges, which do not publish lists. The dossier does not show that lodge ties decided any French policy toward these governments, and the use of Cameroon's state oil money for OSTI was reported, not tested in court.

confirmed_by.title: Jeune Afrique, investigation of Freemasonry in Africa, 2012
Le Monde, 1999, on payments to the Ordre Souverain du Temple Initiatique

implications: Lodges are lawful, and membership is not wrongdoing. What the record shows is a private meeting place shared by African presidents, their ministers and police chiefs, and French Masonic leaders, outside the view of parliaments in Paris or citizens in Libreville and Brazzaville. A Gabonese citizen could not easily know that the president and the police chief led lodges sponsored from France. Several of these presidents ruled for decades. Watch who meets new leaders after a coup or election, whether grand masterships still pass with the presidency, and whether any lodge publishes its officers.

title: Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network

countries.note: Rhodes's trustees, Milner, the Round Table journal (from 1910), Chatham House (1920) and the Pilgrims Society's London branch. Members held the posts of War Cabinet minister (Milner, 1916–18), the prime minister's private secretary (Philip Kerr, 1916–21) and editor of The Times (Geoffrey Dawson, 1912–19 and 1923–41).

Milner was High Commissioner from 1897. After 1902 his young staff ran the Transvaal and Orange River Colony administrations and worked for the 1910 Union. Patrick Duncan, one of them, became Governor-General in 1937.

The Council on Foreign Relations, founded in 1921 after the 1919 Hotel Majestic agreement in Paris, and the Pilgrims Society's New York branch (1903). The CFR's War and Peace Studies project sent memoranda to the State Department from 1939 to 1945.

summary:
This is background to a question that still matters: who staffs the offices where foreign policy is written. It begins with Cecil Rhodes, premier of the Cape Colony, whose wills left his fortune to extend British rule. In 1896 he lost the premiership after the Jameson Raid, a failed armed incursion into the Boer Transvaal; a Commons committee censured him. Carroll Quigley, a Georgetown historian who says he read the group's papers, describes a secret society founded around Rhodes in 1891, with Alfred Milner, later High Commissioner in South Africa, as its chosen heir. That inner society rests on Quigley's account.

The offices are on the record. After the Boer War, Milner brought young Oxford graduates, his 'Kindergarten', into the government of the Transvaal. They pushed for the Union of South Africa of 1910 and founded the Round Table movement, with a journal and groups in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. In 1916 Milner joined Lloyd George's five-man War Cabinet, and Philip Kerr, the Round Table's first editor, became the prime minister's private secretary. Geoffrey Dawson, Milner's former secretary, edited The Times through the 1930s and in 1937 wrote that he removed anything that might hurt German opinion. Kerr, as Lord Lothian, became ambassador to Washington in 1939.

At the 1919 Paris peace conference, Lionel Curtis convened British and American experts who agreed to found institutes of international affairs: Chatham House in London (1920) and the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) in New York (1921). From 1939 the CFR ran confidential planning for the State Department, paid by the Rockefeller Foundation; its own history says a memo on Greenland reached Roosevelt before Germany invaded Denmark. Allen Dulles led one of its groups and later ran the CIA. A 1977 study counted CFR members in about 57% of top foreign-policy posts under Johnson. The Pilgrims Society still welcomes each new US ambassador in London.
uncertain: That these bodies formed one continuous society with an inner circle is Carroll Quigley's reading of papers he was shown; the bodies themselves were public. His description of the CFR as a front for J. P. Morgan & Co., and his claims that the group caused the Boer War or plotted the Jameson Raid, rest on him alone.

confirmed_by.title: Carroll Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment (written 1949, published 1981)

Council on Foreign Relations, centennial history (2021)

implications: Nearly everyone here held office openly, appointed through normal channels. What the record shows is how few doors those channels had. For about half a century, a few hundred people from the same Oxford colleges, the same South African administration and the same London and New York clubs supplied private secretaries, editors, governors and planners on both sides of the Atlantic. Voters chose a party, but the briefing papers its ministers read were often drafted inside this circle. The lesson for today is to look past who wins an election to who staffs the offices, writes the briefings and funds the think tanks.

title: The anticommunist web, 1945–1990

countries.note: Gladio, disclosed by Prime Minister Andreotti on 24 October 1990, and P2, whose 1981 list held the heads of all three intelligence services. Italy is where the stay-behind and lodge networks overlapped most.
The Chilean intelligence service DINA under Manuel Contreras called the founding meeting of Operation Condor in Santiago in November 1975.
CIA support for the stay-behind networks is confirmed in the Italian and Belgian inquiries; Condor's 1976 bombing of Orlando Letelier in Washington was carried out by DINA agents.

summary:
This is the background to much of what the map shows today: a web of secret armies, lodges and intelligence clubs built during the Cold War to fight communism, whose files are still being opened and whose crimes are still being judged.

It began after the Second World War. NATO, the Western military alliance, coordinated secret 'stay-behind' networks: officers and civilians meant to resist a Soviet invasion, with hidden weapons caches. Italy's was called Gladio. Outside a small circle no one knew until 24 October 1990, when Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti told parliament it had existed since the 1950s and handed over a list of 622 civilians. Within months Belgium, Switzerland, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands admitted or investigated their own. Switzerland's P-26 had up to about 1,000 members and spent 54.3 million francs of federal money outside parliament's control; the full report on it stays sealed until 2041.

Around these networks grew others run by the same kind of officers and intelligence men. Licio Gelli's P2 lodge listed 962 names in 1981, including the heads of all three Italian intelligence services; in Argentina its members included a junta admiral and the social welfare minister whose ministry funded the Triple A death squad. From 1975 the secret police of six South American dictatorships joined in Operation Condor to pursue opponents across borders; it killed former Chilean foreign minister Orlando Letelier with a car bomb in Washington in 1976. Its records turned up in a Paraguayan police station in 1992. In 1976 the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Iran and Morocco signed a pact as the 'Safari Club'.

The cases have not closed. In 2019 a Rome appeals court gave 24 life sentences in the Condor case. In 2025 Italy's top court made final a verdict that called Gelli the 'knowing financier' of the 1980 Bologna station bombing, which killed 85 people.
uncertain: No court has found that the stay-behind networks as such carried out the bombings of Italy's 'years of lead'; courts convicted individual neo-fascists and officers, and a Rome court acquitted Gelli and others of conspiracy against the state through P2. A single directing centre for all these bodies is not documented; what is documented is overlapping membership, shared training and money.

confirmed_by.title: European Parliament resolution on Gladio, 22 November 1990
Belgian Senate parliamentary inquiry on stay-behind networks, 1991
US National Security Archive, Operation Condor briefing books

implications: These networks were built for an invasion that never came, and their people, weapons and secrecy were turned on opponents at home. Condor's victims were exiles and dissidents. P2 members headed Italy's intelligence services during years of bombings, and Gelli and a P2-listed intelligence general were convicted over a suitcase of explosives planted to send the Bologna inquiry the wrong way. Most citizens learned these networks existed only in 1990 or later, usually because a government changed, a parliament forced an inquiry or files were found by chance. The lesson for today is practical: secret bodies set up for an emergency tend to outlast it, and the people meant to oversee them often learn last. Watch for sealed records and for courts still ruling on the 1970s and 1980s.

This is the background to how money is still hidden for powerful clients today: a few banks in the 1970s and 1980s grew because governments, a church and intelligence services needed money moved without questions. Banco Ambrosiano in Milan was Italy's largest private bank. Its chairman, Roberto Calvi, was a member of P2, a secret Masonic lodge whose seized 1981 list held 962 names, including ministers, generals and the heads of all three intelligence services. The Vatican Bank (IOR), the Holy See's own bank, was Ambrosiano's main shareholder, and its letters described Panamanian shell companies that had borrowed from Ambrosiano's units as under its control. In 1982 about US$1.3 billion could not be accounted for, and that June Calvi was found hanged under Blackfriars Bridge in London. The Vatican Bank denied liability but paid creditors US$224 million in 1984. Italy's top court ruled in 1987 that the 1929 Lateran Treaty shielded its president, Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, from Italian arrest warrants.

BCCI, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, was founded in 1972 with Gulf money; by 1991 Abu Dhabi's government and ruling family owned 77% of it. A US Senate inquiry found it had secretly owned First American, Washington's largest bank, held about $25 million for Panama's General Manuel Noriega, and handled most of Jamaica's government foreign-currency accounts. It found the CIA kept using BCCI after it knew the bank was criminal. Regulators shut BCCI in July 1991. Former US defence secretary Clark Clifford was indicted, but the state charges were dropped because of his age and health; his partner Robert Altman was acquitted. In Sydney, Nugan Hand Bank, whose staff included retired US generals and admirals, collapsed in 1980.

The thread runs into the present at the Vatican. Its court convicted former IOR president Angelo Caloia of embezzlement in 2021, and Cardinal Angelo Becciu's 2023 conviction over a London property was annulled in March 2026, with a retrial ordered.
uncertain: Australia's Stewart Royal Commission (1985) found no proof that Nugan Hand was a CIA operation. The Vatican paid Ambrosiano's creditors without admitting legal liability, and the five people tried in Rome for Calvi's murder were acquitted in 2007.

confirmed_by.title: US Senate, The BCCI Affair (Kerry–Brown report), 1992
Bank of Italy inquiry into Banco Ambrosiano, 1981–82
Royal Commission of Inquiry into Drug Trafficking (Stewart), 1983–85

implications: These banks were licensed and supervised, and warnings came years before each collapse: the Bank of Italy flagged Ambrosiano in 1978, and US agencies had information about BCCI's hidden ownership from 1981. They stayed open because their customers included a church, intelligence services, a dictator and an oil state. When they failed, depositors and creditors lost money, while the officials who had used them were rarely convicted. Countries also carried the risk: Peru's central bank had $270 million of reserves at BCCI-Panama in 1987. Watch for banks whose clients are governments; they are the slowest to be closed.

title: Sworn brotherhoods that chose who governed

countries.note: Every prime minister and state president from D. F. Malan (1948) to F. W. de Klerk (1989–94) was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society founded in 1918. Its membership list was published by journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom in 1978.

Army officers who later founded the Black Hand killed King Alexander Obrenović in 1903 and its leader, Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis', became head of military intelligence; its rival, the White Hand, put General Petar Živković in power as prime minister in 1929.
IDEA, a secret society of army officers, prepared the April 1967 coup; the colonels ruled until 1974 and were tried in 1975.

The Society of St. Tammany ran New York City's Democratic machine; the Know Nothings won Massachusetts in 1854; the 1920s Klan elected governors in Indiana, Colorado and Oregon and helped send Hugo Black to the Senate and then the Supreme Court.

summary:
This is background: in some countries a sworn society did not slip into the government, it chose who formed one. The plainest case is South Africa. The Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918, counted every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 among its members, from D. F. Malan, the first apartheid prime minister, to F. W. de Klerk. A 1979 report put it at about 12,000 members and said all but two cabinet ministers belonged, with 49 members in key posts at the state broadcaster. The heads of the security service and the army were members too, and the society's own chairman became a cabinet minister in 1980.

In the Balkans the societies were made of army officers. In 1903 Serbian officers killed King Alexander Obrenović; in 1911 their leader, Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis', founded the Black Hand and was made chief of military intelligence in 1913. He was shot in 1917 after a treason trial that Serbia's Supreme Court overturned in 1953. A rival White Hand officer, Petar Živković, became Yugoslavia's prime minister in 1929. In Greece, several leaders of the 1967 coup belonged to IDEA, a secret officers' society; they were convicted of high treason in 1975.

In North America lodges built political machines. The Tammany Society ran New York City; its leader 'Boss' Tweed was convicted in 1873. The secret Know Nothing order won the Massachusetts governorship and legislature in 1854. Orangemen held Toronto's mayoralty for a century. In the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan backed governors in Oregon, Colorado, Indiana and Alabama, and Hugo Black, a former Klansman, was confirmed to the US Supreme Court in 1937. The thread reaches the present: in 2014 an FBI inquiry found a deputy police chief and an officer in Fruitland Park, Florida, had been involved with the Klan.
uncertain: Membership is documented for each officeholder here, but how much of each government's policy was decided inside the society rather than in cabinet is a matter of historians' judgement, strongest for the Broederbond. Some links, such as a Klan alliance with Saskatchewan's 1929 government, were alleged and denied, and Quigley's Rhodes society claims rest on him alone.

confirmed_by.title: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)
Greek junta trials, 1975
Indiana and Colorado Klan histories; Hugo Black's radio address, 1 October 1937

implications: Where one society chooses the leaders, an election only decides which of its members holds the job. South Africans who were not white Afrikaner men had no route into the Broederbond, so for 46 years they had no route into the circle that picked their rulers. The same thing appears on a smaller scale in a city run by a lodge, a state run by the Klan, or an army run by a secret officers' society. Because the members simply are the government, nothing looks out of place from outside. Watch for the same signs today: one private body supplying the ministers, police chiefs and broadcasters at once.

summary:
This is background to a question governments still argue about today: who pays for the civic groups that work across borders. In the early Cold War the CIA, the US foreign intelligence agency, quietly paid for a set of bodies that looked like private, independent organisations. The Congress for Cultural Freedom, founded in West Berlin in 1950 and run from Paris by a CIA officer, Michael Josselson, had offices in 35 countries and published more than 20 magazines, including Encounter in London. The Asia Foundation began in 1951 as the CIA-funded Committee for a Free Asia; a 1966 CIA memo called it "a Central Intelligence Agency proprietary". The US National Student Association, the federation of college student governments, took CIA money until a former staffer exposed it in Ramparts magazine in 1967. Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty, broadcasting from Munich into the Soviet bloc, ran on CIA money until 1971–72.

The money also reached other countries' elections. Historian Anthony Carew found that the CIA channelled funds through the American Federation of Labor's Free Trade Union Committee, starting with Italy's 1948 election. In Brazil a parliamentary inquiry examined how the Brazilian Institute of Democratic Action paid for opposition campaigns in 1962; in 1977 the former US ambassador admitted the United States had funded the opposition. In 1976 the Senate's Church Committee found CIA money in at least 108 of 700 large grants made by 164 US foundations in 1963–66.

From 1983 much of this work moved into the open through the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), funded by Congress. Its founder, Allen Weinstein, said in 1991 that "a lot of what we do today was done covertly 25 years ago by the CIA." That history carries into the present: Russia banned the NED as "undesirable" in 2015, and China sanctioned it in 2019, both calling it a front.
uncertain: How far this money changed particular election results is mostly unproven, and the claim that AIFLD-trained unionists helped bring about Brazil's 1964 coup rests on the institute's own director, whom historians think overstated it. Russia's and China's descriptions of the NED as a front are their governments' assertions, not findings by an independent body.

confirmed_by.title: US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence Activities (Church Committee), Final Report, Book I, 1976
Washington Post, 22 September 1991 (Weinstein interview)
Ramparts, March 1967

implications: The people reading the magazines, attending the conferences and voting in those elections thought they were dealing with independent civic groups. Nobody told them a foreign intelligence service was paying, and the same money backed particular parties and candidates in other countries. Today most funding of this kind is done openly and published, through the NED and others. But the old secret funding gives governments a ready reason to treat any foreign-funded group as suspect, and Russia and China now use it to ban groups they dislike. For a reader, the practical question about any civic group, magazine or broadcaster is who pays for it and whether that is disclosed.

title: Lenders, aid programmes and trained technocrats
roles: Country whose economy was run by the trainees or advisers
case_role: Country whose economy was run by the trainees or advisers

countries.note: The Ford Foundation paid for Indonesian economists to train at Berkeley; the US aid agency (ICA, later USAID) funded the 1956 agreement between the University of Chicago and Chile's Catholic University; the US Treasury ran the Saudi Joint Commission from a Saudi-funded trust account.

timeline.event: Chile Project links University of Chicago and Catholic University of Chile under US aid
