summary:
This is background to how a country's economy can come to be run by people trained or paid through another country's programmes, a thread that continues today in the conditions lenders attach to loans. In the late 1950s the US Ford Foundation paid for University of Indonesia economists to take doctorates at the University of California, Berkeley. When Suharto took power in 1966 they became his economic team. Widjojo Nitisastro ran the planning agency BAPPENAS from 1967 to 1983, and Ali Wardhana was finance minister, the post that controls the state's money, from 1968 to 1983. Their programme cut inflation from 650% to 13% by 1969 and opened Indonesia to foreign investors.

In Chile, from 1955 a US aid scheme, later funded by the Ford Foundation, linked Santiago's Catholic University with the University of Chicago, training 126 Chilean students by 1973. Their 189-page plan, "El ladrillo" ("the brick"), became the junta's economic programme in 1975, and its graduates took the top posts: Sergio de Castro ran the economy and then finance ministries until the 1982 debt crisis, and Miguel Kast became Central Bank governor.

In Saudi Arabia, a joint commission set up in 1974 and co-chaired by the US Treasury Secretary supplied US advisers paid from a Saudi account in the US Treasury; a 1979 US audit found it recycled oil money into US goods and services.

John Perkins, a former chief economist at the Boston engineering firm Chas. T. Main, wrote in 2004 that his job was to inflate growth forecasts so countries would take large loans for US-built projects. The New York Times found his career described accurately but no evidence that the National Security Agency recruited him, and the State Department called much of it fabricated. The loans of this era had to be repaid by later governments, and the Loan Conditions map on this site follows that story through the lenders' own terms.
uncertain: Perkins's account of an organised scheme to load countries with debt for US companies is his own and is disputed, and the NSA link he describes is unconfirmed. The Indonesian and Chilean economists held office openly under military governments; whether their training made them instruments of US policy is a matter of interpretation.

confirmed_by.title: US General Accounting Office report on the US–Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation, 1979
New York Times, 'Economic Hit Man' review, 2005

implications: No secret oath is needed when a country's economic ministries are staffed by people trained, paid or advised through another country's institutions. The choices those ministers made, such as privatisation, opening to foreign capital and borrowing for large projects, shaped the lives of millions who never voted for them; in Indonesia and Chile they served military governments. Later governments were left to repay the loans. For a reader today, the things to look for are who trained a country's finance and central-bank officials, who pays its foreign advisers, and which outside lenders set conditions on its budget.

title: Exposure, purge and reversal

timeline.event: US Senate Church Committee begins hearings on intelligence abuses
Italian police find the P2 list at Licio Gelli's villa (17 March)
Andreotti discloses Gladio to the Italian parliament (24 October)
Regulators in seven countries close BCCI (5 July)
Paraguay's 'Archives of Terror' found in Lambaré (22 December)
Turkey begins mass dismissals after the 15 July coup attempt
Australia passes its foreign interference and foreign influence transparency laws
Tokyo District Court orders the Unification Church dissolved (25 March)

summary:
This is the background to how infiltration stories tend to unfold, and it helps in reading the present-day cases on this map. The record moves in three steps. First, something exposes a network, often by accident. On 17 March 1981 Italian financial police, searching a factory in a case about another banker, found a list of 962 members of a secret lodge called P2: 44 members of parliament, 195 military officers and the heads of all three intelligence services. During the search the commander of the financial police phoned the officer leading it to say, 'I am in those lists too.' In 1990 Italy's military intelligence confirmed that a secret NATO 'stay-behind' network, Gladio, had 622 members, and Switzerland's parliament found its own hidden cadre organisation, P-26.

Second, a government bans the group or purges its members, sometimes with a law written for the purpose. Italy dissolved P2 by law in 1982. Egypt declared the Muslim Brotherhood a terrorist organisation in 2013, and Jordan banned it in April 2025 although its party held the most seats in parliament. The day after Turkey's 2016 coup attempt, its judicial council removed 2,745 judges for alleged links to the Gülen movement; about 15,000 military personnel and 23,000 police followed.

Third, years later, courts often narrow or reverse the findings. Rome courts acquitted Licio Gelli and others of conspiracy through P2 in 1994 and 1996. In Turkey all 236 remaining Sledgehammer defendants were acquitted in 2015 after the evidence was found to be forged, and in 2016 the Ergenekon convictions were overturned for lack of evidence the organisation existed. Brazil's Supreme Court annulled Lula's Car Wash convictions in 2021. The cycle is still running: after the Unification Church's ties to ruling-party lawmakers came out in 2022, Japan's courts ordered it dissolved in 2025 and upheld the order in March 2026.
uncertain: The three steps are a pattern in this map's records, not a rule: many exposures led to no purge, and many purges were never reviewed by a court. An acquittal or annulment often rests on procedure or lack of proof and does not by itself settle whether a network existed.

confirmed_by.title: Italian Law no. 17 of 25 January 1982
Turkish Constitutional Court and Court of Cassation rulings on Ergenekon and Sledgehammer, 2015–16

implications: Exposure rarely comes from the bodies meant to watch for it. It comes from a raid on something else, a car crash like the one at Susurluk in Turkey in 1996 that put an MP, a police chief and a wanted gunman in the same car, a leak, or a change of government. What follows is shaped by politics as well as evidence: purges can be wide enough to take in people who were never members, evidence can be forged, as in Sledgehammer, and reversals can let real members back. Ordinary people are left unsure which version to believe. With any new infiltration story, ask which stage it is at, who exposed it and why then, and whether a court has tested it yet.
